title: Periods in the first few years: what is normal, and when does a girl need a doctor?
behavior_type: الدورة الشهرية في أول سنوات البلوغ — الطبيعي وعلامات الخطر
reference_info: الأكاديمية الأمريكية لطب الأطفال (HealthyChildren.org): Menstrual Disorders in Teens · KidsDoc: Vaginal Bleeding · NHS: Periods · Starting your periods · Heavy periods · Irregular periods · Period pain — اطّلعنا عليها في 5 أكتوبر 2026
text_original: This unit draws on public health guidance pages accessed on 5 October 2026. We restated their facts in our own words rather than quoting their text: (1) AAP, “Menstrual Disorders in Teens”: periods usually start between 10 and 15; irregularity is common in the first 2 to 3 years because the ovaries do not release an egg every month; a gap longer than 3 months is rare even in the first two years; bleeding less than every 21 days or more than every 45 days is abnormal in adolescents; the interval is measured from the first day of one period to the first day of the next; one or two years after the first period, pain affects 50 to 75 out of every 100 girls; bleeding is heavy if it lasts longer than 7 days, soaks one or more pads in an hour or two for several hours, requires two pads together, or requires changing at night; heavy bleeding may be the first sign of a blood clotting disorder; see a doctor if periods have not started by 15, are absent for more than 3 months, remain irregular after two years, become irregular after being regular, or pain limits activities or causes school absence; conditions are treated with medicines chosen by the doctor. (2) AAP KidsDoc, “Vaginal Bleeding”: bleeding before puberty is abnormal and needs examination; a girl may skip one or two periods after the first; there is often no pain in the first year; bleeding is excessive if it lasts longer than 7 days, reaches 6 fully soaked pads or more per day (seek care within 24 hours), occurs less than every 21 days, or occurs between periods; call emergency services if she faints or is too weak to stand; go to emergency care if two pads per hour are fully soaked for two or more hours and bleeding continues, or bleeding is accompanied by severe abdominal pain; seek medical care now if one pad per hour is fully soaked for 6 or more hours, or there is new paleness, bruising or nosebleeding without injury, or any bleeding before puberty. (3) NHS, “Starting your periods”: most girls start at about 12, though periods may start at 8; they usually start about two years after breast development begins; see a doctor if they have not started by 15, or by 13 if there are no other signs of puberty; the first period may be short, and the body needs months to become regular. (4) NHS, “Periods”: most women have periods every 21 to 35 days, lasting 2 to 7 days, with the heaviest bleeding in the first two days; total blood loss is about 20 to 90 ml, or one to 5 tablespoons. (5) NHS, “Heavy periods”: signs include changing a pad every hour or two, using two types of menstrual product together, a period longer than 7 days, or clots larger than about 2.5 cm. (6) NHS, “Irregular periods”: irregularity is more likely at the start of puberty; recording periods in a notebook or app helps. (7) NHS, “Period pain”: pain usually lasts up to 3 days; a warm bath, a wrapped warm compress on the abdomen, massage of the abdomen and back, gentle exercise such as walking, and appropriate pain medicines can ease it; seek an urgent appointment if pain is severe or worse than usual and pain medicines have not helped. (8) milestones.json and ramadan_family.json: “She learns the rules of purification from a trusted female teacher or scholar”; “A girl does not fast on the days of menstruation and makes them up after Ramadan without being embarrassed; the details of the rulings should be sought from scholars.”
text_simplified:
What is normal for periods in the first few years?
• Periods usually start between 10 and 15, at about 12 for most girls, and usually about two years after breast development begins.
• Irregularity is common in the first 2 to 3 years because the body does not yet release an egg every month; she may skip one or two periods after the first. Recording the date and duration of each period in a notebook or app helps.
• A period usually lasts 2 to 7 days, with the heaviest bleeding in the first two days. Total blood loss is small: about 20 to 90 ml, approximately one to 5 tablespoons.
• According to the NHS, most women have periods every 21 to 35 days. In adolescents, however, an interval shorter than 21 days or longer than 45 days needs a doctor's assessment. Measure the interval from the first day of one period to the first day of the next.
• Many girls experience period pain a year or two after periods start; it usually lasts up to 3 days. A warm bath, a warm compress on the abdomen, massage of the abdomen and back, or gentle exercise such as walking can help. If she needs pain medicine, ask the doctor or pharmacist what is suitable for her.

She does not fast during menstruation and makes up those days after Ramadan without being embarrassed. She learns the rules of menstruation concerning prayer, fasting and purification from a trusted female teacher or scholar. If you are unsure whether bleeding is menstruation, ask scholars.

When to see a doctor:
• Periods have not started by 15, or by 13 without any other sign of puberty.
• A period is absent for more than 3 months, periods remain irregular two years after starting, or previously regular periods become irregular.
• Periods occur less than every 21 days or more than every 45 days, last longer than 7 days, or there is bleeding between periods.
• Bleeding is heavy: changing a pad every hour or two for several hours, needing two pads together or changes at night, or passing clots larger than about 2.5 cm.
• Pain prevents school attendance or usual activities, or becomes severe and relief measures do not help.
• Seek medical care now: one pad per hour is fully soaked for 6 or more hours, new paleness, unexplained bruising or nosebleeding, or any bleeding before signs of puberty. Heavy bleeding may be the first sign of a blood clotting disorder.
• Seek care within 24 hours if 6 or more pads are fully soaked in a day.
• Go to emergency care immediately if two pads per hour are fully soaked for two or more hours and bleeding continues, or bleeding is accompanied by severe abdominal pain. Call emergency services if she faints or is too weak to stand.
